## 4. Contact is a second-order event

### 4.1 Instantaneous contact

**Definition 4.1 (Contemporaneity and contact).** Sites $i \ne j$ are
*contemporaneous* in outcome $f$ if $f(i) = f(j) \ne \ast$. The event
$$
\mathrm{Contact} = \{\, f : \exists\, i \ne j,\ f(i) = f(j) \ne \ast \,\}
$$
is the event that the cosmos ever contains two civilizations born in the same
epoch.

**Lemma 4.2 (Exact two-site law).** For $i \ne j$ and any epochs $e, e'$,
$$
\mathbb{P}\bigl(f(i) = e \ \wedge\ f(j) = e'\bigr) = \left(\frac{p}{T}\right)^{2}.
$$

*Proof sketch.* Theorem 2.5 with $B_i = \{e\}$, $B_j = \{e'\}$, and $B_k$ full for
$k \notin \{i,j\}$; the two singled-out factors contribute $p/T$ each and all
others contribute $1$. $\square$

**Lemma 4.3 (Pairwise contact bound).** For $0 \le p \le 1$, $T \ge 1$, $i \ne j$,
$$
\mathbb{P}\bigl(f(i) = f(j) \ne \ast\bigr) \;\le\; \frac{p^2}{T}.
$$

*Proof sketch.* The event is contained in the union over epochs $e$ of the events
$\{f(i) = f(j) = e\}$. Each has probability $(p/T)^2$ by Lemma 4.2; the union
bound over $T$ epochs gives $T \cdot (p/T)^2 = p^2/T$. $\square$

**Theorem 4.4 (Contact is quadratically rare).** For $0 \le p \le 1$ and
$T \ge 1$,
$$
\boxed{\ \mathbb{P}(\mathrm{Contact}) \;\le\; \frac{(N^2 - N)\,p^2}{T}\ }
$$

*Proof sketch.* $\mathrm{Contact}$ is the union of the pairwise events over the
$N^2 - N$ ordered pairs of distinct sites. Apply the union bound and Lemma 4.3.
$\square$

**Corollary 4.5 (Contact controlled by the squared Drake expectation).**
$$
\mathbb{P}(\mathrm{Contact}) \;\le\; \frac{(Np)^2}{T} \;=\; \frac{\mathbb{E}[X]^2}{T}.
$$

**Remark 4.6 (Two structural readings).**
- **Quadratic in abundance.** Contact is a *pairwise* event, so its probability
  scales as the square of the first moment. Halving $p$ quarters the chance of a
  meeting. Optimism about contact is therefore far more fragile than optimism
  about existence.
- **Inversely proportional to time.** More epochs means *less* contact. In the
  pigeonhole picture, additional time supplies additional holes into which the
  same small number of pigeons is scattered. The vast age of the universe, usually
  cited as an argument for contact, appears in the denominator.

### 4.2 Contact through a lifetime window

Real civilizations persist. We model this with Drake's lifetime factor.

**Definition 4.7 (Temporal window).** For $L \ge 1$, epochs $a, b$ are *within a
window of width $L$* if $a + L > b$ and $b + L > a$, i.e. $|a - b| < L$. The event
$$
\mathrm{Contact}_L = \{\, f : \exists\, i \ne j,\ f(i), f(j) \ne \ast,\ |f(i) - f(j)| < L \,\}
$$
is the event that two civilizations are ever mutually detectable.

**Lemma 4.8 (Window fibre count).** For a fixed epoch $a$, the number of epochs
$b$ with $|a - b| < L$ is at most $2L - 1$.

*Proof sketch.* Such $b$ lie in the integer interval $(a - L, a + L)$, which
contains at most $2L - 1$ integers; the map $b \mapsto b + L - 1 - a$ injects them
into $\{0, 1, \dots, 2L-2\}$. $\square$

**Lemma 4.9 (Window pair count).** Among the $T^2$ ordered pairs of epochs, at
most $T(2L-1)$ lie within a window of width $L$.

*Proof sketch.* Partition the pairs by their first coordinate and apply Lemma 4.8
to each of the $T$ fibres. $\square$

**Theorem 4.10 (Windowed contact bound).** For $0 \le p \le 1$, $T \ge 1$,
$L \ge 1$,
$$
\boxed{\ \mathbb{P}(\mathrm{Contact}_L) \;\le\; (N^2 - N)\,\frac{(2L-1)\,p^2}{T}.\ }
$$

*Proof sketch.* For a fixed pair $i \ne j$, the windowed pair event is the union
over the window-compatible epoch pairs $(e,e')$ of the events
$\{f(i) = e,\ f(j) = e'\}$, each of probability $(p/T)^2$ by Lemma 4.2. By Lemma
4.9 there are at most $T(2L-1)$ such pairs, giving
$T(2L-1)(p/T)^2 = (2L-1)p^2/T$ per site pair. A second union bound over the
$N^2 - N$ ordered site pairs completes the proof. $\square$

**Remark 4.11 (Lifetime is a weak lever).** Setting $L = 1$ recovers Theorem 4.4.
Note the asymmetry of the exponents: $L$ appears **linearly**, $p$
**quadratically**. Doubling civilization lifetimes roughly doubles contact
probability; doubling the abundance quadruples it. In the Drake literature $L$ is
customarily treated as the dominant unknown; in the mathematics of *contact* it is
the weakest of the available levers.

## 5. Pigeonhole combinatorics, correctly oriented

This section is purely deterministic: no probability appears. Let $C$ be a finite
set of civilizations with a birth-epoch assignment
$\mathrm{ep} : C \to \{1,\dots,T\}$, and write $c = |C|$.

**Theorem 5.1 (Quantitative pigeonhole).** If $T \cdot n < c$, then some epoch $e$
satisfies $\#\{\,\gamma \in C : \mathrm{ep}(\gamma) = e\,\} > n$.

*Proof sketch.* If every fibre had at most $n$ elements, then
$c = \sum_e |\mathrm{fibre}(e)| \le T n < c$, a contradiction. $\square$

**Corollary 5.2 (Forced contact).** If $c > T$, there exist distinct
$\gamma \ne \delta$ in $C$ with $\mathrm{ep}(\gamma) = \mathrm{ep}(\delta)$:
contact is combinatorially forced.

*Proof sketch.* Theorem 5.1 with $n = 1$ produces an epoch carrying at least two
civilizations. $\square$

**Theorem 5.3 (Sharpness of the threshold).** If $c \le T$, there exists an
assignment $\mathrm{ep} : C \to \{1,\dots,T\}$ that is injective, hence in which no
two civilizations are contemporaries.

*Proof sketch.* An injection $C \hookrightarrow \{1,\dots,T\}$ exists precisely
when $c \le T$. $\square$

Thus $c = T$ is the exact pigeonhole threshold: above it, contact is forced; at or
below it, pigeonhole forces nothing at all. In the Fermi setting $c$ is at most a
handful and $T \approx 4.5 \times 10^9$; the forcing hypothesis fails by nine
orders of magnitude.

**Theorem 5.4 (Dual pigeonhole: empty holes).**
$$
\#\{\, e : \text{no } \gamma \in C \text{ has } \mathrm{ep}(\gamma) = e \,\} \;\ge\; T - c .
$$

*Proof sketch.* The occupied epochs are exactly the image
$\mathrm{ep}(C)$, of cardinality at most $c$. Complement within the $T$ epochs.
$\square$

**Corollary 5.5 (Pigeonhole predicts emptiness).** If $c < T$, at least one epoch
is completely empty; and the number of empty epochs is at least $T - c$, which is
overwhelmingly large in the Fermi regime.

### 5.1 Coupling to the probabilistic model

**Definition 5.6 (Empty epochs of an outcome).** For $f \in \Omega_{N,T}$ let
$$
E(f) = \#\{\, e : f(i) \ne e \text{ for all } i \,\}
$$
be the number of epochs in which no site hosts a newborn civilization.

**Lemma 5.7 (Pointwise dual pigeonhole).** For every outcome $f$,
$$
E(f) \;\ge\; T - X(f).
$$

*Proof sketch.* Apply Theorem 5.4 with $C$ the set of civilized sites, of
cardinality $X(f)$, and $\mathrm{ep}$ the induced birth-epoch map. (If no site is
civilized, all $T$ epochs are empty and the inequality is immediate.) $\square$

**Theorem 5.8 (Expected emptiness).** For $0 \le p \le 1$ and $T \ge 1$,
$$
\boxed{\ \mathbb{E}[E] \;\ge\; T - Np .\ }
$$

*Proof sketch.* Take expectations in Lemma 5.7, using linearity, normalization
($\mathbb{E}[T] = T$), and Theorem 3.3 ($\mathbb{E}[X] = Np$). Pointwise
nonnegativity of the weights makes the inequality survive the averaging. $\square$

**Remark 5.9.** When $Np < 1$, Theorem 5.8 says that **all but at most one of the
$T$ epochs of cosmic history are expected to be completely empty**. This is the
precise sense in which the pigeonhole principle, applied with honest counts,
predicts an empty universe rather than a crowded one.

---

## 6. The Fermi dichotomy

**Theorem 6.1 (Fermi dichotomy).** Let $0 \le p \le 1$, $T \ge 1$, and write
$\mathcal{E} = Np$ for the Drake expectation. If $\mathcal{E} < 1$ then
simultaneously:

1. $\mathbb{P}(\text{lifeless}) \ge 1 - \mathcal{E} > 0$;
2. $\mathbb{P}(\mathrm{Contact}) \le 1/T$;
3. $\mathbb{E}[E] > T - 1$.

*Proof sketch.* (1) is Theorem 3.6 together with $\mathcal{E} < 1$. (2) follows
from Corollary 4.5 and $\mathcal{E}^2 \le 1$. (3) is Theorem 5.8 with
$Np < 1$. $\square$

Three qualitatively distinct predictions — emptiness, non-contact, temporal
vacancy — follow from the single hypothesis that the first moment is below one. No
Great Filter, zoo hypothesis, or self-destruction mechanism is invoked or needed.

---

## 7. Cosmological instantiation

Fix conservative but defensible parameters:

$$
N = 10^{10}, \qquad T = 4.5 \times 10^{9}, \qquad p = 10^{-11}.
$$

Here $N$ is an order-of-magnitude estimate of habitable-zone worlds accessible to
the argument, $T$ counts one-year epochs over $4.5$ Gyr, and $p$ is the
probability that a habitable world ever produces a technological civilization. The
value of $p$ is a product of several contingent evolutionary transitions
(abiogenesis, eukaryogenesis, multicellularity, encephalization, technology); if
each has probability of order $10^{-2}$ to $10^{-3}$, their product falls in this
range.

**Theorem 7.1 (Expected count).** With these parameters,
$\mathbb{E}[X] = Np = 1/10$.

**Theorem 7.2 (Lifeless with high probability).**
$\mathbb{P}(\text{lifeless}) \ge 9/10$.

**Theorem 7.3 (Existence sandwich).**
$$
0.095 \;=\; \tfrac{19}{200} \;\le\; \mathbb{P}(\text{somebody exists}) \;\le\; \tfrac{1}{10} \;=\; 0.1 .
$$
In particular the model is not vacuous: someone exists with probability roughly
one in ten, and the first-moment answer is correct to within $5 \times 10^{-3}$.

**Theorem 7.4 (Contact).**
$\mathbb{P}(\mathrm{Contact}) \le 10^{-11}$.

**Theorem 7.5 (Contact with generous lifetimes).** Granting every civilization a
detectability lifetime of $L = 10^{4}$ epochs (ten thousand years),
$$
\mathbb{P}(\mathrm{Contact}_{10^4}) \;\le\; 10^{-7}.
$$

**Theorem 7.6 (Empty epochs).**
$$
\mathbb{E}[E] \;\ge\; 4\,500\,000\,000 - \tfrac{1}{10} .
$$

All six follow by substituting the parameter values into Theorems 3.3, 3.6,
Corollary 3.8, Theorem 4.4, Theorem 4.10, and Theorem 5.8 respectively, and
performing exact rational arithmetic.

**Summary of the instantiation.**

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Expected number of civilizations $\mathbb{E}[X]$ | $0.1$ exactly |
| $\mathbb{P}(\text{lifeless})$ | $\ge 0.9$ |
| $\mathbb{P}(\text{somebody exists})$ | $\in [0.095,\ 0.1]$ |
| $\mathbb{P}(\text{contact}, L=1)$ | $\le 10^{-11}$ |
| $\mathbb{P}(\text{contact}, L=10^4)$ | $\le 10^{-7}$ |
| Expected empty epochs (out of $4.5\times 10^9$) | $\ge 4\,499\,999\,999.9$ |

We observe silence. The model predicts silence with probability $0.9$ and predicts
that, even conditionally on someone existing, contact is essentially impossible.
Observation and prediction agree.

---

## 8. Exact computational corroboration

The estimates above are inequalities. To confirm they are neither vacuous nor
grossly lossy, the model can be enumerated *exactly* in rational arithmetic for
small $(N,T,p)$, since $|\Omega_{N,T}| = (T+1)^N$ is small. Representative exact
values:

| Parameters | Quantity | Exact value | Proved bound |
|---|---|---|---|
| $N{=}3, T{=}2, p{=}\tfrac15$ | total mass | $1$ | $=1$ (normalization) |
| $N{=}3, T{=}2, p{=}\tfrac15$ | $\mathbb{P}(\mathrm{Contact})$ | $\tfrac{7}{125} = 0.0560$ | $\le \tfrac{3}{25} = 0.12$ |
| $N{=}4, T{=}3, p{=}\tfrac1{10}$ | $\mathbb{P}(\mathrm{Contact})$ | $\tfrac{191}{10000} = 0.0191$ | $\le \tfrac{1}{25} = 0.04$ |
| $N{=}3, T{=}2, p{=}\tfrac15$ | $\mathbb{P}(\text{lifeless})$ | $\tfrac{64}{125} = 0.512$ | $= (1-p)^3$; $\ge \tfrac25$ |
| $N{=}4, T{=}3, p{=}\tfrac1{10}$ | $\mathbb{P}(\text{somebody})$ | $\tfrac{3439}{10000} = 0.3439$ | $\in [0.32,\ 0.40]$ |
| $N{=}3, T{=}2, p{=}\tfrac15$ | $\mathbb{E}[E]$ | $\tfrac{729}{500} = 1.458$ | $\ge \tfrac75 = 1.4$ |
| $N{=}4, T{=}3, p{=}\tfrac1{10}$ | $\mathbb{E}[E]$ | $\tfrac{707281}{270000} \approx 2.6196$ | $\ge \tfrac{13}{5} = 2.6$ |

Two structural facts are visible in the numbers.

**Contact decays like $1/T$.** With $N = 3$, $p = 1/5$ fixed, the exact contact
probabilities for $T = 2, 3, 4$ are $\tfrac{7}{125} = 0.0560$,
$\tfrac{43}{1125} = 0.0382$, $\tfrac{29}{1000} = 0.0290$ — tracking the predicted
inverse-linear decay in the number of epochs.

**The union bound loses exactly a factor $2$ in the two-site case.** For $N = 2$,
$T = 5$, $p = 1/2$, the exact contact probability is $\tfrac{1}{20}$ while the
bound gives $\tfrac{1}{10}$: precisely the slack from counting *ordered* rather
than unordered pairs. This confirms the estimates are tight up to this explicit
constant.

## 9. Discussion

### 9.1 What is proved, and what is assumed

The theorems are unconditional statements about the model. The *cosmological
conclusions* are conditional on the parameter values, and above all on $p$. The
mathematics does not determine $p$; nothing currently known does.

What the mathematics does establish is that **no additional explanatory mechanism
is required**. The Fermi paradox literature is largely a catalogue of proposed
suppression mechanisms — Great Filters past or future, the zoo hypothesis, the
dark forest, self-destruction, transcension — each designed to reconcile a "large
predicted population" with an empty sky. But the Drake calculation never predicted
a large population; it computed a mean. Theorem 3.6 and Corollary 3.8 show that
when that mean is below one, emptiness is the *modal* outcome, and Theorem 6.1
shows that non-contact and temporal vacancy come along for free.

### 9.2 The inference runs backwards

Because Corollary 3.8 is two-sided, silence is *informative about $p$* rather than
about mechanisms. If $\mathbb{P}(\text{somebody}) \in [Np - \tfrac12(Np)^2, Np]$,
then observing no neighbours is a likelihood-ratio statement about $Np$ directly.
A century of null results is a Bayesian update on a single scalar. This reframes
SETI: it is not a search for an anomaly's explanation but an estimator for $p$.

### 9.3 Structural lessons independent of the parameters

Four conclusions survive whatever $p$ turns out to be.

1. **The Drake number is a first moment.** When small, it should be read as the
   probability that anyone exists, not as a headcount (Interpretation 3.9).
2. **Contact scales as the square of abundance.** Existence is first order;
   meeting is second order (Theorem 4.4).
3. **Time is in the denominator.** Cosmic longevity spreads a fixed expected
   population over more epochs, *reducing* contact probability (Remark 4.6).
4. **Lifetime is a linear lever; abundance is quadratic.** Arguments for a
   populated, communicative galaxy should target $p$, not $L$ (Remark 4.11).

### 9.4 Limitations of the model

The model deliberately omits several features.

- **Spatial structure.** Sites are exchangeable; there is no notion of distance,
  light travel time, or causal reachability. Adding a metric can only *reduce*
  contact probability, so the bounds remain valid as upper bounds on any
  spatially-embedded refinement.
- **Colonization and propagation.** A civilization that seeds daughter
  civilizations violates site independence. This is the most substantive
  omission: percolation-type models with expansion can produce contact
  probabilities far above the independent-site bounds once the branching factor
  exceeds one. The present analysis is a statement about the *non-expanding*
  regime.
- **Uniform birth epochs.** Real habitability is time-inhomogeneous (metallicity
  ramps, gamma-ray-burst sterilization). Non-uniform epoch distributions
  concentrate births and *increase* contact probability by a factor equal to the
  effective inverse participation ratio $T \sum_e q_e^2$ of the epoch
  distribution $q$.
- **One civilization per site.** Repeated independent origins on a single world
  would multiply $p$; the model absorbs this into $p$ by definition.
- **Upper bounds only for contact.** Theorems 4.4 and 4.10 bound contact from
  above. A matching lower bound requires a second-moment (variance) computation;
  see §10.

### 9.5 Relation to occupancy theory

Readers will recognize the classical *occupancy problem*: $c$ balls into $T$ boxes,
with the number of empty boxes concentrating around $T e^{-c/T}$. Our Theorem 5.8
is the deterministic, distribution-free shadow of that asymptotic, and it holds
with no independence assumption on the epoch assignment whatsoever — which is what
lets it be coupled to the probabilistic first moment without any additional
hypotheses. The Fermi regime $c \ll T$ is the extreme sparse corner of occupancy
theory, where essentially every box is empty and the interesting statistic is not
the number of empty boxes but the number of *collisions* — which is exactly the
birthday-problem quantity governed by $c^2/T$, matching Corollary 4.5 on the nose.

## 10. Future directions

### 10.1 A sharp second-moment threshold for contact

**Conjecture.** Contact undergoes a sharp threshold at $N^2p^2L/T = 1$: if
$N^2p^2L/T \to 0$ then $\mathbb{P}(\mathrm{Contact}_L) \to 0$, while if
$N^2p^2L/T \to \infty$ *and* $Np \to \infty$ then
$\mathbb{P}(\mathrm{Contact}_L) \to 1$.

The contact indicator is a sum of pair indicators whose pairwise correlations are
$O(p^3)$; the second-moment (Paley–Zygmund) method should convert the proved
first-moment upper bound into a matching lower bound. The missing ingredient is
the variance estimate $\mathrm{Var}[Y] \le \mathbb{E}[Y] + O(N^3p^3L^2/T)$ for the
pair-count $Y$. If confirmed, the Fermi question acquires a **phase diagram**
rather than a single verdict, with $N^2p^2L/T$ as the order parameter. If refuted,
the correlation structure of birth epochs matters at leading order — itself a
substantive finding.

### 10.2 Pigeonhole rigidity for contact-free schedules

**Conjecture.** For $c \le T$, the number of contact-free schedules of $c$
civilizations into $T$ epochs with lifetime window $L$ is exactly
$$
T\bigl(T - (2L-1)\bigr)\bigl(T - 2(2L-1)\bigr)\cdots\bigl(T - (c-1)(2L-1)\bigr)
$$
whenever $(c-1)(2L-1) < T$, and zero otherwise; consequently a contact-free
schedule exists **if and only if** $(c-1)(2L-1) < T$.

The insight is that a window of width $L$ converts the pigeonhole count from "one
hole per pigeon" to "one *interval* of $2L-1$ holes per pigeon", a
circular-interval packing problem with an exact product formula. The interval count
is already available (Lemma 4.9), and the $L = 1$ case is Theorem 5.3.

### 10.3 Further programme

- **Spatially embedded models.** Place sites in a metric space and require causal
  contact within light-travel time; derive the corresponding percolation
  threshold.
- **Colonization dynamics.** Replace independent sites with a branching process
  and identify the critical branching factor at which the contact bound fails.
- **Non-uniform epochs.** Quantify the exact inflation factor $T\sum_e q_e^2$ for
  realistic habitability histories.
- **Inverse problem.** Given $k$ centuries of null observations, produce a rigorous
  confidence upper bound on $p$ using the two-sided estimate of Corollary 3.8.

---

## 11. Conclusion

The Fermi paradox is not a paradox. Written down carefully, the Drake calculation
is a first moment, and a first moment below one predicts — with quantitative,
two-sided precision — an empty cosmos, a vanishing probability of contact, and a
history almost every epoch of which contains nobody at all. The pigeonhole
principle, applied with the correct counts, does not force encounters; in its dual
form it *guarantees empty holes*, at least $T - Np$ of them in expectation.

Under conservative parameters the expected number of technological civilizations
in the observable universe is $0.1$; the cosmos is lifeless with probability at
least $0.9$; contact ever occurring has probability below $10^{-11}$, and below
$10^{-7}$ even granting every civilization ten thousand years of detectability.

We observe silence. The mathematics predicts silence. The correct response is not
to seek a hidden mechanism, but to recognize a small number multiplied by a large
one, and to update our estimate of that small number accordingly.

\begin{abstract}
We construct an explicit finite product probability space modelling a universe of
$N$ habitable sites observed over $T$ discrete epochs, in which each site
independently produces a technological civilization with probability $p$, born in
a uniformly random epoch. Within this model we prove that the Drake equation is
\emph{exactly} a first moment: the expected number of technological civilizations
is $Np$, with no dependence on $T$. We show that the probability of a completely
lifeless cosmos is exactly $(1-p)^N$, that Bernoulli's inequality bounds this below
by $1-Np$, and that a matching second-order Bonferroni estimate
$(1-p)^N \le 1 - Np + \tfrac12 N^2p^2$ pins the probability that anyone exists to
the interval $[Np - \tfrac12 (Np)^2,\, Np]$. Consequently the Drake number, when
small, is not a population count but a probability. We then prove that
\emph{contact}---the existence of two contemporaneous civilizations---is second
order in the small parameter: $\Prob(\Contact) \le (N^2-N)p^2/T \le (Np)^2/T$, and,

$\Prob(\Contact) \le (N^2-N)(2L-1)p^2/T$. Lifetime therefore enters linearly while
abundance enters quadratically. On the combinatorial side we establish the correct
orientation of the pigeonhole principle: contact is forced only when the number of
civilizations exceeds $T$ (a sharp threshold, since contact-free schedules exist
below it), whereas the \emph{dual} pigeonhole guarantees at least $T-c$ empty
epochs, yielding $\Exp[\#\text{empty epochs}] \ge T - Np$. Combining these gives the
\emph{Fermi dichotomy}: whenever $Np<1$, a lifeless cosmos has probability at least
$1-Np>0$, contact has probability at most $1/T$, and more than $T-1$ epochs are
expected to be empty. Instantiating with $N=10^{10}$, $T=4.5\times 10^{9}$,

least $4.5\times 10^9 - 0.1$ empty epochs in expectation. The Fermi paradox is
thereby dissolved: observed silence is the model's prediction, not an anomaly
requiring exotic resolution.

\section{Introduction}

\subsection{The question and its logical status}

Fermi's question---\emph{where is everybody?}---acquires the status of a paradox
only when paired with a quantitative claim that many civilizations \emph{should} be
visible. That claim is invariably some version of the Drake equation
\[
\mathcal{N} = R_* \cdot f_p \cdot n_e \cdot f_\ell \cdot f_i \cdot f_c \cdot L,
\]
a product of astrophysical and biological rate factors. Sixty years of literature
have debated the factors. Comparatively little attention has been paid to a prior
question: \emph{what kind of quantity is $\mathcal{N}$?}

We argue that $\mathcal{N}$ is, and can only be, an expectation---a first moment of
a counting random variable. This is not a philosophical remark but a theorem in a
precisely specified model, and it has sharp consequences. A first moment below one
is not evidence of a suppression mechanism; it is a direct statement that the
typical realization of the underlying random experiment contains \emph{nothing at
all}.

\subsection{Pigeonhole, in the correct direction}

The pigeonhole principle is frequently invoked informally in this setting to force
coincidences: ``with so many planets and so much time, somebody must have
overlapped with us.'' The invocation has the orientation backwards. Pigeonhole
forces a collision only when pigeons outnumber holes. Here the pigeons are
civilizations (expected count possibly below $1$) and the holes are epochs of
cosmic history (count $\sim 4.5\times 10^{9}$). The applicable statement is the
\emph{dual}: $c$ objects placed into $T$ boxes leave at least $T-c$ boxes empty.
Under Fermi-regime numbers this predicts a cosmos in which essentially every epoch
is vacant. The silence is the prediction.

\begin{enumerate}

\item The Drake equation as a first moment (\S\ref{sec:drake}): $\Exp[X]=Np$

\section{The model}\label{sec:model}

\subsection{Sample space and weights}

\begin{definition}[Cosmos]
Fix integers $N \ge 0$ (habitable sites) and $T \ge 1$ (epochs). The sample space
is the finite set
\[
\Om = \bigl\{\, f : \{1,\dots,N\} \to \{\ast\} \cup \{1,\dots,T\} \,\bigr\},
\]
where $f(i) = \ast$ means site $i$ never produced a technological civilization and
$f(i) = e$ means site $i$ produced exactly one civilization, born in epoch $e$.
Thus $|\Om| = (T+1)^N$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Local weight]
For $p \in [0,1]$ define $w(\ast) = 1-p$ and $w(e) = p/T$ for $1 \le e \le T$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Outcome weight and probability]
The weight of an outcome is $W(f) = \prod_{i=1}^{N} w(f(i))$, and the probability
of an event $A \subseteq \Om$ is $\Prob(A) = \sum_{f \in A} W(f)$.
\end{definition}

The interpretation: sites are independent; each is barren with probability $1-p$
and otherwise produces a civilization whose birth epoch is uniform on
$\{1,\dots,T\}$.

\begin{lemma}[Local normalization]\label{lem:localnorm}
For $T \ge 1$, $\sum_{x} w(x) = (1-p) + T\cdot \tfrac{p}{T} = 1$, and $w(x)\ge 0$
whenever $0 \le p \le 1$.
\end{lemma}

\subsection{The engine: cylinder factorization}

\begin{theorem}[Cylinder factorization]\label{thm:cylinder}
For any subsets $B_i \subseteq \{\ast\} \cup \{1,\dots,T\}$, $1 \le i \le N$,
\[
\Prob\bigl(\{ f : f(i) \in B_i \text{ for all } i \}\bigr)
= \prod_{i=1}^{N} \ \sum_{x \in B_i} w(x).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The event is exactly the product set $B_1 \times \cdots \times B_N$. Its total
weight is $\sum_{f \in \prod_i B_i} \prod_i w(f(i))$, and the distributive law for
finite products of finite sums---$\prod_i \sum_{x\in B_i}$ expands into a sum over
choice functions---identifies this with $\prod_i \sum_{x\in B_i} w(x)$. Outcomes
outside the product set contribute zero to the indicator sum.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Normalization]\label{cor:norm}
Taking every $B_i$ to be the full state set gives $\Prob(\Om) = 1$. Hence $\Prob$
is a probability measure and $\Prob(A) + \Prob(A^c) = 1$ for all $A$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{lemma}[Monotonicity, nonnegativity, union bound]\label{lem:union}
For $0 \le p \le 1$: $\Prob(A) \ge 0$; $A \subseteq B$ implies
$\Prob(A) \le \Prob(B)$; and for any finite family $\{A_x\}_{x\in S}$,
\[
\Prob\Bigl(\bigcup_{x\in S} A_x\Bigr) \le \sum_{x\in S}\Prob(A_x).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Nonnegativity and monotonicity are pointwise statements about indicator functions
against a nonnegative weight. For the union bound, the indicator of a union is
dominated pointwise by the sum of indicators; summing over $\Om$ and exchanging the
order of summation gives the claim.
\end{proof}

\section{The Drake equation is a first moment}\label{sec:drake}

\begin{definition}[Civilization count]
For $f \in \Om$ let $X(f) = \#\{ i : f(i) \ne \ast \}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Marginal law of a site]\label{lem:marginal}
For each $i$ and any $T\ge 1$, $\Prob(f(i)\ne\ast) = p$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:cylinder} with $B_i$ the set of all epochs (excluding
$\ast$) and $B_j$ the full state set for $j \ne i$. The $i$-th factor is
$T\cdot(p/T) = p$; every other factor is $1$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:localnorm}. The epoch
degree of freedom integrates out precisely because a civilization must be born in
\emph{some} epoch.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Drake as a first moment]\label{thm:drake}
For $T \ge 1$,
\[
\Exp[X] \;=\; N p.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Write $X = \sum_{i=1}^N \mathbf 1[f(i)\ne\ast]$. Exchanging the finite sums defining
the expectation and the counting decomposition, each term becomes
$\Prob(f(i)\ne\ast) = p$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:marginal}. Summing over $i$ gives $Np$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The number of epochs $T$ does not appear. Lengthening cosmic history does not change
how many civilizations one expects---only how thinly they are distributed in time.
This is why the $T$-dependence reappears, in the \emph{denominator}, for contact
events (\S\ref{sec:contact}).
\end{remark}

\begin{theorem}[Probability of a lifeless cosmos]\label{thm:lifeless}
$\Prob\bigl(f(i)=\ast \text{ for all } i\bigr) = (1-p)^N$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Theorem~\ref{thm:cylinder} with every $B_i = \{\ast\}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Bernoulli / emptiness bound]\label{thm:bernoulli}
For $p \le 1$, $\Prob(\text{lifeless}) = (1-p)^N \ge 1 - Np$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Bernoulli's inequality $(1+x)^n \ge 1+nx$ for $x \ge -2$, with $x = -p$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Second-order Bonferroni bound]\label{thm:bonferroni}
For $0 \le p \le 1$ and all $n \ge 0$,
\[
(1-p)^n \;\le\; 1 - np + \tfrac12 n^2 p^2.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induction on $n$. The base case is an identity. For the step, multiply the inductive
hypothesis by $(1-p)\ge 0$ and compare with the target at $n+1$; the difference is a
polynomial in $p$ and $n$ whose nonnegativity follows from $p \ge 0$, $n \ge 0$ and
$p \le 1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Two-sided first-moment estimate]\label{cor:sandwich}
For $0 \le p \le 1$,
\[
Np - \tfrac12 (Np)^2 \;\le\; \Prob(\text{somebody exists}) \;\le\; Np.
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The upper bound is the union bound (Lemma~\ref{lem:union}) applied to the $N$
single-site events, each of probability $p$. The lower bound is complementation of
Theorem~\ref{thm:bonferroni} via Corollary~\ref{cor:norm}.
\end{proof}

\begin{interpretation}
When $Np \ll 1$, the Drake number is \emph{the probability that we have any
neighbours at all}, correct to relative error $O(Np)$. It is not a population count.
Reading a small $\mathcal N$ as ``we expect a fraction of a civilization'' is a
category error; the correct reading is ``with probability
$1 - \mathcal N + O(\mathcal N^2)$ there is nobody.''
\end{interpretation}

\begin{theorem}[Emptiness is typical]
If $p \le 1$ and $Np < 1$ then $\Prob(\text{lifeless}) \ge 1 - Np > 0$. In
particular, once $Np < \tfrac12$, a completely lifeless cosmos is the majority
outcome.
\end{theorem}

\section{Contact is a second-order event}\label{sec:contact}

\subsection{Instantaneous contact}

\begin{definition}[Contemporaneity and contact]
Sites $i \ne j$ are \emph{contemporaneous} in $f$ if $f(i) = f(j) \ne \ast$. Put
\[
\Contact = \{\, f : \exists\, i \ne j,\ f(i) = f(j) \ne \ast \,\}.
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Exact two-site law]\label{lem:twosite}
For $i \ne j$ and any epochs $e,e'$,
$\Prob\bigl(f(i)=e \wedge f(j)=e'\bigr) = (p/T)^2$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Theorem~\ref{thm:cylinder} with $B_i = \{e\}$, $B_j = \{e'\}$ and $B_k$ full for
$k \notin \{i,j\}$; the two singled-out factors contribute $p/T$ each and all others
contribute $1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Pairwise contact bound]\label{lem:pairwise}
For $0 \le p \le 1$, $T \ge 1$, $i \ne j$:
$\Prob\bigl(f(i) = f(j) \ne \ast\bigr) \le p^2/T$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The event is contained in the union over epochs $e$ of $\{f(i)=f(j)=e\}$; each has
probability $(p/T)^2$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:twosite}, and the union bound over $T$ epochs
gives $T(p/T)^2 = p^2/T$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Contact is quadratically rare]\label{thm:contact}
For $0 \le p \le 1$ and $T \ge 1$,
\[
\Prob(\Contact) \;\le\; \frac{(N^2-N)\,p^2}{T}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$\Contact$ is the union of the pairwise events over the $N^2-N$ ordered pairs of
distinct sites; apply Lemma~\ref{lem:union} and Lemma~\ref{lem:pairwise}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Contact controlled by the squared Drake expectation]\label{cor:contactE}
$\Prob(\Contact) \le (Np)^2/T = \Exp[X]^2/T$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{remark}[Two structural readings]
\emph{Quadratic in abundance.} Contact is a pairwise event, so its probability scales
as the square of the first moment; halving $p$ quarters the chance of a meeting.
\emph{Inversely proportional to time.} More epochs means \emph{less} contact: in the
pigeonhole picture, additional time supplies additional holes into which the same
small number of pigeons is scattered. The vast age of the universe, usually cited as
an argument for contact, appears in the denominator.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Contact through a lifetime window}

\begin{definition}[Temporal window]
For $L \ge 1$, epochs $a,b$ are \emph{within a window of width $L$} if $a + L > b$
and $b + L > a$, i.e.\ $|a-b| < L$. Put
\[
\Contact_L = \{\, f : \exists\, i \ne j,\ f(i),f(j)\ne\ast,\ |f(i)-f(j)| < L \,\}.
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Window fibre count]\label{lem:fibre}
For a fixed epoch $a$, the number of epochs $b$ with $|a-b| < L$ is at most $2L-1$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Such $b$ lie in the integer interval $(a-L, a+L)$, which contains at most $2L-1$
integers; the map $b \mapsto b + L - 1 - a$ injects them into $\{0,\dots,2L-2\}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Window pair count]\label{lem:pairs}
Among the $T^2$ ordered pairs of epochs, at most $T(2L-1)$ lie within a window of
width $L$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Partition the pairs by their first coordinate and apply Lemma~\ref{lem:fibre} to each
of the $T$ fibres.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Windowed contact bound]\label{thm:window}
For $0 \le p \le 1$, $T \ge 1$, $L \ge 1$,
\[
\Prob(\Contact_L) \;\le\; (N^2-N)\,\frac{(2L-1)\,p^2}{T}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
For a fixed pair $i \ne j$, the windowed pair event is the union over
window-compatible epoch pairs $(e,e')$ of the events $\{f(i)=e,\, f(j)=e'\}$, each of
probability $(p/T)^2$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:pairs} there are at most $T(2L-1)$ such
pairs, giving $(2L-1)p^2/T$ per site pair; a second union bound over the $N^2-N$
ordered site pairs completes the proof.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Lifetime is a weak lever]
Setting $L=1$ recovers Theorem~\ref{thm:contact}. Note the asymmetry of the
exponents: $L$ appears linearly, $p$ quadratically. Doubling civilization lifetimes
roughly doubles contact probability; doubling abundance quadruples it. In the Drake
literature $L$ is customarily treated as the dominant unknown; in the mathematics of
contact it is the weakest of the available levers.
\end{remark}

\section{Pigeonhole combinatorics, correctly oriented}\label{sec:pigeon}

This section is purely deterministic. Let $C$ be a finite set of civilizations with a
birth-epoch assignment $\ep : C \to \{1,\dots,T\}$, and write $c = |C|$.

\begin{theorem}[Quantitative pigeonhole]\label{thm:qpigeon}
If $T\cdot n < c$, then some epoch $e$ satisfies
$\#\{\gamma \in C : \ep(\gamma) = e\} > n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
If every fibre had at most $n$ elements then $c = \sum_e |\ep^{-1}(e)| \le Tn < c$, a
contradiction.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Forced contact]
If $c > T$, there exist distinct $\gamma \ne \delta$ in $C$ with
$\ep(\gamma) = \ep(\delta)$: contact is combinatorially forced.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Sharpness of the threshold]\label{thm:sharp}
If $c \le T$, there exists an injective assignment $\ep : C \to \{1,\dots,T\}$, hence
one in which no two civilizations are contemporaries.
\end{theorem}

Thus $c = T$ is the exact pigeonhole threshold. In the Fermi setting $c$ is at most a
handful and $T \approx 4.5\times 10^9$; the forcing hypothesis fails by nine orders of
magnitude.

\begin{theorem}[Dual pigeonhole: empty holes]\label{thm:dual}
$\#\{\, e : \text{no } \gamma \in C \text{ has } \ep(\gamma) = e \,\} \ge T - c$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The occupied epochs are exactly the image $\ep(C)$, of cardinality at most $c$;
complement within the $T$ epochs.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Coupling to the probabilistic model}

\begin{definition}[Empty epochs of an outcome]
For $f \in \Om$ let $E(f) = \#\{\, e : f(i) \ne e \text{ for all } i \,\}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Pointwise dual pigeonhole]\label{lem:pointwise}
For every outcome $f$, $E(f) \ge T - X(f)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:dual} with $C$ the set of civilized sites, of cardinality
$X(f)$, and $\ep$ the induced birth-epoch map. If no site is civilized, all $T$
epochs are empty and the inequality is immediate.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Expected emptiness]\label{thm:empty}
For $0 \le p \le 1$ and $T \ge 1$,
\[
\Exp[E] \;\ge\; T - Np.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Take expectations in Lemma~\ref{lem:pointwise}, using linearity, normalization and
Theorem~\ref{thm:drake}. Pointwise nonnegativity of the weights makes the inequality
survive the averaging.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
When $Np < 1$, Theorem~\ref{thm:empty} says that all but at most one of the $T$
epochs of cosmic history are expected to be completely empty. This is the precise
sense in which the pigeonhole principle, applied with honest counts, predicts an
empty universe rather than a crowded one.
\end{remark}

\section{The Fermi dichotomy}\label{sec:dichotomy}

\begin{theorem}[Fermi dichotomy]\label{thm:dichotomy}
Let $0 \le p \le 1$, $T \ge 1$, and write $\mathcal E = Np$. If $\mathcal E < 1$ then
simultaneously:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\Prob(\text{lifeless}) \ge 1 - \mathcal E > 0$;
\item $\Prob(\Contact) \le 1/T$;
\item $\Exp[E] > T - 1$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
(1) is Theorem~\ref{thm:bernoulli} with $\mathcal E < 1$. (2) follows from
Corollary~\ref{cor:contactE} and $\mathcal E^2 \le 1$. (3) is Theorem~\ref{thm:empty}
with $Np < 1$.
\end{proof}

Three qualitatively distinct predictions---emptiness, non-contact, temporal
vacancy---follow from the single hypothesis that the first moment is below one. No
Great Filter, zoo hypothesis, or self-destruction mechanism is invoked or needed.

\section{Cosmological instantiation}\label{sec:cosmo}

Fix
\[
N = 10^{10}, \qquad T = 4.5 \times 10^{9}, \qquad p = 10^{-11}.
\]
Here $N$ is an order-of-magnitude estimate of habitable-zone worlds accessible to the
argument, $T$ counts one-year epochs over $4.5$\,Gyr, and $p$ is the probability that
a habitable world ever produces a technological civilization---a product of several
contingent evolutionary transitions (abiogenesis, eukaryogenesis, multicellularity,
encephalization, technology).

\begin{theorem}[Cosmological consequences]
With these parameters:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\Exp[X] = Np = 1/10$ exactly;
\item $\Prob(\text{lifeless}) \ge 9/10$;
\item $19/200 = 0.095 \le \Prob(\text{somebody exists}) \le 1/10$;
\item $\Prob(\Contact) \le 10^{-11}$;
\item $\Prob(\Contact_{10^4}) \le 10^{-7}$;
\item $\Exp[E] \ge 4\,500\,000\,000 - 1/10$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Substitute the parameter values into Theorems~\ref{thm:drake}, \ref{thm:bernoulli},
Corollary~\ref{cor:sandwich}, Theorems~\ref{thm:contact}, \ref{thm:window} and
\ref{thm:empty} respectively, and perform exact rational arithmetic.
\end{proof}

\section{Exact computational corroboration}\label{sec:evidence}

The estimates above are inequalities. To confirm they are neither vacuous nor grossly
lossy, the model can be enumerated exactly in rational arithmetic for small

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

\subsection{What is proved, and what is assumed}

The theorems are unconditional statements about the model. The cosmological
conclusions are conditional on the parameters, and above all on $p$. The mathematics
does not determine $p$; nothing currently known does.

What the mathematics does establish is that \emph{no additional explanatory mechanism
is required}. The Fermi paradox literature is largely a catalogue of proposed
suppression mechanisms---Great Filters past or future, the zoo hypothesis, the dark
forest, self-destruction, transcension---each designed to reconcile a ``large
predicted population'' with an empty sky. But the Drake calculation never predicted a
large population; it computed a mean. Theorem~\ref{thm:bernoulli} and
Corollary~\ref{cor:sandwich} show that when that mean is below one, emptiness is the
modal outcome, and Theorem~\ref{thm:dichotomy} shows that non-contact and temporal
vacancy come along for free.

\subsection{The inference runs backwards}

Because Corollary~\ref{cor:sandwich} is two-sided, silence is \emph{informative about
$p$} rather than about mechanisms: observing no neighbours is a likelihood statement
about $Np$ directly. A century of null results is a Bayesian update on a single
scalar. This reframes the search for extraterrestrial intelligence as an estimator for
$p$ rather than a search for an anomaly's explanation.

\subsection{Structural lessons independent of the parameters}

\begin{enumerate}
\item The Drake number is a first moment; when small it should be read as the
      probability that anyone exists, not as a headcount.
\item Contact scales as the square of abundance: existence is first order, meeting is
      second order.
\item Time is in the denominator: cosmic longevity spreads a fixed expected population
      over more epochs, reducing contact probability.
\item Lifetime is a linear lever; abundance is quadratic. Arguments for a populated,
      communicative galaxy should target $p$, not $L$.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Limitations}

The model omits spatial structure (adding a metric and light-travel constraints can
only reduce contact probability, so the bounds remain valid); colonization and
propagation (which violate site independence and are the most substantive omission,
since branching processes with branching factor above one can exceed the
independent-site bounds); time-inhomogeneous habitability (non-uniform epoch
distributions $q$ inflate contact probability by the inverse participation ratio
$T\sum_e q_e^2$); and multiple independent origins per site (absorbed into $p$ by
definition). Finally, Theorems~\ref{thm:contact} and~\ref{thm:window} are upper bounds
only; a matching lower bound requires a variance computation (\S\ref{sec:future}).

\subsection{Relation to occupancy theory}

Readers will recognize the classical occupancy problem: $c$ balls into $T$ boxes, with
the number of empty boxes concentrating around $Te^{-c/T}$. Theorem~\ref{thm:empty} is
the deterministic, distribution-free shadow of that asymptotic, holding with no
independence assumption on the epoch assignment---which is what allows it to be
coupled to the probabilistic first moment without additional hypotheses. The Fermi
regime $c \ll T$ is the extreme sparse corner of occupancy theory, where essentially
every box is empty and the interesting statistic is the number of \emph{collisions},
the birthday-problem quantity governed by $c^2/T$---matching
Corollary~\ref{cor:contactE} exactly.

\section{Future directions}\label{sec:future}

\subsection{A sharp second-moment threshold for contact}

\begin{conjecture}
Contact undergoes a sharp threshold at $N^2p^2L/T = 1$: if $N^2p^2L/T \to 0$ then
$\Prob(\Contact_L) \to 0$, while if $N^2p^2L/T \to \infty$ and $Np \to \infty$ then
$\Prob(\Contact_L) \to 1$.
\end{conjecture}

The contact indicator is a sum of pair indicators whose pairwise correlations are
$O(p^3)$, so the second-moment (Paley--Zygmund) method should convert the proved
first-moment upper bound into a matching lower bound. The missing ingredient is the
variance estimate $\operatorname{Var}[Y] \le \Exp[Y] + O(N^3p^3L^2/T)$ for the pair
count $Y$. If confirmed, the Fermi question acquires a phase diagram rather than a
single verdict, with $N^2p^2L/T$ as order parameter; if refuted, the correlation
structure of birth epochs matters at leading order.

\subsection{Pigeonhole rigidity for contact-free schedules}

\begin{conjecture}
For $c \le T$, the number of contact-free schedules of $c$ civilizations into $T$
epochs with lifetime window $L$ is exactly
\[
T\bigl(T-(2L-1)\bigr)\bigl(T-2(2L-1)\bigr)\cdots\bigl(T-(c-1)(2L-1)\bigr)
\]
whenever $(c-1)(2L-1) < T$, and zero otherwise; consequently a contact-free schedule
exists if and only if $(c-1)(2L-1) < T$.
\end{conjecture}

The insight is that a window of width $L$ converts the pigeonhole count from ``one hole
per pigeon'' to ``one \emph{interval} of $2L-1$ holes per pigeon''---a circular-interval
packing problem with an exact product formula. The interval count is already available
(Lemma~\ref{lem:pairs}) and the case $L=1$ is Theorem~\ref{thm:sharp}.

\subsection{Further programme}

Spatially embedded models with causal contact constraints and their percolation
thresholds; colonization dynamics as branching processes, identifying the critical
branching factor at which the contact bound fails; exact inflation factors
$T\sum_e q_e^2$ for realistic habitability histories; and the inverse problem of
converting $k$ centuries of null observations into a rigorous confidence upper bound
on $p$ via Corollary~\ref{cor:sandwich}.

\section{Conclusion}

The Fermi paradox is not a paradox. Written down carefully, the Drake calculation is a
first moment, and a first moment below one predicts---with quantitative, two-sided
precision---an empty cosmos, a vanishing probability of contact, and a history almost
every epoch of which contains nobody at all. The pigeonhole principle, applied with the
correct counts, does not force encounters; in its dual form it guarantees empty holes,
at least $T - Np$ of them in expectation.

Under conservative parameters the expected number of technological civilizations in the
observable universe is $0.1$; the cosmos is lifeless with probability at least $0.9$;
contact ever occurring has probability below $10^{-11}$, and below $10^{-7}$ even
granting every civilization ten thousand years of detectability.

We observe silence. The mathematics predicts silence. The correct response is not to
seek a hidden mechanism, but to recognize a small number multiplied by a large one, and
to update our estimate of that small number accordingly.

and the weight of an outcome is the product of local weights.  Since

(T+1)^N possible cosmoi.

Results demonstrated
--------------------
  1. Normalisation:            sum over all outcomes of W(f) = 1
  2. Drake as a first moment:  E[#civilizations] = N * p          (exact)
  3. Lifeless cosmos:          P(lifeless) = (1-p)^N >= 1 - N*p   (Bernoulli)
  4. Existence sandwich:       N p - (N p)^2 / 2 <= P(somebody) <= N p
  5. Contact bound:            P(contact) <= (N^2 - N) p^2 / T
  6. Windowed contact bound:   P(contact_L) <= (N^2 - N)(2L-1) p^2 / T
  7. Dual pigeonhole:          E[#empty epochs] >= T - N p
  8. Fermi dichotomy and the cosmological instantiation

arithmetic (fractions.Fraction), so the printed comparisons are exact, not
Monte-Carlo estimates.

Run:  python3 demo.py

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from itertools import product
from typing import Callable, Iterator, List, Optional, Tuple

Outcome = Tuple[Optional[int], ...]


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Core model: exact enumeration in rational arithmetic
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def enumerate_cosmoi(n_sites: int, n_epochs: int) -> Iterator[Outcome]:
    """Yield every outcome f : sites -> {None} u {0,...,n_epochs-1}."""
    states: List[Optional[int]] = [None] + list(range(n_epochs))
    for combo in product(states, repeat=n_sites):
        yield combo


def site_weight(state: Optional[int], n_epochs: int, p: Fraction) -> Fraction:
    """Local weight: 1 - p for a barren site, p / T for a birth in a given epoch."""
    if state is None:
        return Fraction(1) - p
    return p / Fraction(n_epochs)


def outcome_weight(f: Outcome, n_epochs: int, p: Fraction) -> Fraction:
    """Product of the local weights over all sites."""
    w = Fraction(1)
    for state in f:
        w *= site_weight(state, n_epochs, p)
    return w


def probability(
    n_sites: int,
    n_epochs: int,
    p: Fraction,
    event: Callable[[Outcome], bool],
) -> Fraction:
    """Exact probability of a decidable event, by full enumeration."""
    total = Fraction(0)
    for f in enumerate_cosmoi(n_sites, n_epochs):
        if event(f):
            total += outcome_weight(f, n_epochs, p)
    return total


def expectation(
    n_sites: int,
    n_epochs: int,
    p: Fraction,
    statistic: Callable[[Outcome], int],
) -> Fraction:
    """Exact expectation of an integer-valued statistic, by full enumeration."""
    total = Fraction(0)
    for f in enumerate_cosmoi(n_sites, n_epochs):
        total += outcome_weight(f, n_epochs, p) * Fraction(statistic(f))
    return total


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Events and statistics
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def civ_count(f: Outcome) -> int:
    """Number of sites hosting a civilization."""
    return sum(1 for s in f if s is not None)


def is_lifeless(f: Outcome) -> bool:
    """No site ever produced a civilization."""
    return all(s is None for s in f)


def somebody_exists(f: Outcome) -> bool:
    """At least one site produced a civilization."""
    return any(s is not None for s in f)


def has_contact(f: Outcome) -> bool:
    """Two distinct sites are civilized and born in the SAME epoch."""
    n = len(f)
    for i in range(n):
        if f[i] is None:
            continue
        for j in range(n):
            if i != j and f[j] is not None and f[i] == f[j]:
                return True
    return False


def has_window_contact(f: Outcome, lifetime: int) -> bool:
    """Two distinct civilizations are born within `lifetime` epochs of each other."""
    n = len(f)
    for i in range(n):
        if f[i] is None:
            continue
        for j in range(n):
            if i != j and f[j] is not None and abs(f[i] - f[j]) < lifetime:
                return True
    return False


def empty_epoch_count(f: Outcome, n_epochs: int) -> int:
    """Number of epochs in which no site hosts a newborn civilization."""
    occupied = {s for s in f if s is not None}
    return n_epochs - len(occupied)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Proved bounds (closed forms)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def drake_expectation(n_sites: int, p: Fraction) -> Fraction:
    """E[#civilizations] = N * p  (exact; independent of T)."""
    return Fraction(n_sites) * p


def lifeless_exact(n_sites: int, p: Fraction) -> Fraction:
    """P(lifeless) = (1 - p)^N."""
    return (Fraction(1) - p) ** n_sites


def bernoulli_lower(n_sites: int, p: Fraction) -> Fraction:
    """P(lifeless) >= 1 - N p."""
    return Fraction(1) - Fraction(n_sites) * p


def bonferroni_upper(n_sites: int, p: Fraction) -> Fraction:
    """(1 - p)^N <= 1 - N p + N^2 p^2 / 2."""
    e = Fraction(n_sites) * p
    return Fraction(1) - e + e * e / 2


def contact_bound(n_sites: int, n_epochs: int, p: Fraction) -> Fraction:
    """P(contact) <= (N^2 - N) p^2 / T."""
    return Fraction(n_sites ** 2 - n_sites) * p * p / Fraction(n_epochs)


def window_contact_bound(
    n_sites: int, n_epochs: int, p: Fraction, lifetime: int
) -> Fraction:
    """P(contact_L) <= (N^2 - N)(2L - 1) p^2 / T."""
    return (
        Fraction(n_sites ** 2 - n_sites)
        * Fraction(2 * lifetime - 1)
        * p
        * p
        / Fraction(n_epochs)
    )


def empty_epochs_bound(n_sites: int, n_epochs: int, p: Fraction) -> Fraction:
    """E[#empty epochs] >= T - N p."""
    return Fraction(n_epochs) - Fraction(n_sites) * p

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from itertools import product
from typing import Callable, Iterator, List, Optional, Tuple

Outcome = Tuple[Optional[int], ...]


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Core model: exact enumeration in rational arithmetic
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def enumerate_cosmoi(n_sites: int, n_epochs: int) -> Iterator[Outcome]:
    """Yield every outcome f : sites -> {None} u {0,...,n_epochs-1}."""
    states: List[Optional[int]] = [None] + list(range(n_epochs))
    for combo in product(states, repeat=n_sites):
        yield combo


def site_weight(state: Optional[int], n_epochs: int, p: Fraction) -> Fraction:
    """Local weight: 1 - p for a barren site, p / T for a birth in a given epoch."""
    if state is None:
        return Fraction(1) - p
    return p / Fraction(n_epochs)


def outcome_weight(f: Outcome, n_epochs: int, p: Fraction) -> Fraction:
    """Product of the local weights over all sites."""
    w = Fraction(1)
    for state in f:
        w *= site_weight(state, n_epochs, p)
    return w


def probability(
    n_sites: int,
    n_epochs: int,
    p: Fraction,
    event: Callable[[Outcome], bool],
) -> Fraction:
    """Exact probability of a decidable event, by full enumeration."""
    total = Fraction(0)
    for f in enumerate_cosmoi(n_sites, n_epochs):
        if event(f):
            total += outcome_weight(f, n_epochs, p)
    return total


def expectation(
    n_sites: int,
    n_epochs: int,
    p: Fraction,
    statistic: Callable[[Outcome], int],
) -> Fraction:
    """Exact expectation of an integer-valued statistic, by full enumeration."""
    total = Fraction(0)
    for f in enumerate_cosmoi(n_sites, n_epochs):
        total += outcome_weight(f, n_epochs, p) * Fraction(statistic(f))
    return total


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Events and statistics
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def civ_count(f: Outcome) -> int:
    """Number of sites hosting a civilization."""
    return sum(1 for s in f if s is not None)


def is_lifeless(f: Outcome) -> bool:
    """No site ever produced a civilization."""
    return all(s is None for s in f)


def somebody_exists(f: Outcome) -> bool:
    """At least one site produced a civilization."""
    return any(s is not None for s in f)


def has_contact(f: Outcome) -> bool:
    """Two distinct sites are civilized and born in the SAME epoch."""
    n = len(f)
    for i in range(n):
        if f[i] is None:
            continue
        for j in range(n):
            if i != j and f[j] is not None and f[i] == f[j]:
                return True
    return False


def has_window_contact(f: Outcome, lifetime: int) -> bool:
    """Two distinct civilizations are born within `lifetime` epochs of each other."""
    n = len(f)
    for i in range(n):
        if f[i] is None:
            continue
        for j in range(n):
            if i != j and f[j] is not None and abs(f[i] - f[j]) < lifetime:
                return True
    return False


def empty_epoch_count(f: Outcome, n_epochs: int) -> int:
    """Number of epochs in which no site hosts a newborn civilization."""
    occupied = {s for s in f if s is not None}
    return n_epochs - len(occupied)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Proved bounds (closed forms)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def drake_expectation(n_sites: int, p: Fraction) -> Fraction:
    """E[#civilizations] = N * p  (exact; independent of T)."""
    return Fraction(n_sites) * p


def lifeless_exact(n_sites: int, p: Fraction) -> Fraction:
    """P(lifeless) = (1 - p)^N."""
    return (Fraction(1) - p) ** n_sites


def bernoulli_lower(n_sites: int, p: Fraction) -> Fraction:
    """P(lifeless) >= 1 - N p."""
    return Fraction(1) - Fraction(n_sites) * p


def bonferroni_upper(n_sites: int, p: Fraction) -> Fraction:
    """(1 - p)^N <= 1 - N p + N^2 p^2 / 2."""
    e = Fraction(n_sites) * p
    return Fraction(1) - e + e * e / 2


def contact_bound(n_sites: int, n_epochs: int, p: Fraction) -> Fraction:
    """P(contact) <= (N^2 - N) p^2 / T."""
    return Fraction(n_sites ** 2 - n_sites) * p * p / Fraction(n_epochs)


def window_contact_bound(
    n_sites: int, n_epochs: int, p: Fraction, lifetime: int
) -> Fraction:
    """P(contact_L) <= (N^2 - N)(2L - 1) p^2 / T."""
    return (
        Fraction(n_sites ** 2 - n_sites)
        * Fraction(2 * lifetime - 1)
        * p
        * p
        / Fraction(n_epochs)
    )


def empty_epochs_bound(n_sites: int, n_epochs: int, p: Fraction) -> Fraction:
    """E[#empty epochs] >= T - N p."""
    return Fraction(n_epochs) - Fraction(n_sites) * p


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Reporting helpers
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def show(label: str, value: Fraction, width: int = 46) -> str:
    return f"{label:<{width}} {str(value):>18}  = {float(value):.8f}"


def rule(title: str = "") -> None:
    if title:
        print("\n" + "=" * 78)
        print(title)
        print("=" * 78)
    else:
        print("-" * 78)

def demo_normalisation() -> None:
    rule("1. NORMALISATION  --  the weights really do define a probability measure")
    for n, t, p in [(3, 2, Fraction(1, 5)), (4, 3, Fraction(1, 10))]:
        mass = probability(n, t, p, lambda f: True)
        print(f"  N={n}, T={t}, p={p}:  total mass over {(t+1)**n:>4} outcomes = {mass}")
        assert mass == 1, "weights must sum to one"
    print("  OK: total mass is exactly 1 in every case.")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstration 2: the Drake equation is a first moment
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def demo_drake_first_moment() -> None:
    rule("2. THE DRAKE EQUATION IS A FIRST MOMENT:  E[#civilizations] = N p")
    print("  Note in particular that the answer does NOT depend on T.")
    print()
    for n, t, p in [(3, 2, Fraction(1, 5)), (3, 5, Fraction(1, 5)),
                    (4, 3, Fraction(1, 10)), (4, 7, Fraction(1, 10))]:
        exact = expectation(n, t, p, civ_count)
        closed = drake_expectation(n, p)
        print(f"  N={n}, T={t}, p={p}:  enumerated = {exact}   "
              f"closed form N p = {closed}   match = {exact == closed}")
        assert exact == closed


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstration 3: emptiness is typical
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def demo_emptiness() -> None:
    rule("3. EMPTINESS IS TYPICAL:  P(lifeless) = (1-p)^N >= 1 - N p")
    for n, t, p in [(3, 2, Fraction(1, 5)), (4, 3, Fraction(1, 10)),
                    (5, 4, Fraction(1, 20))]:
        exact = probability(n, t, p, is_lifeless)
        closed = lifeless_exact(n, p)
        lower = bernoulli_lower(n, p)
        upper = bonferroni_upper(n, p)
        print(f"\n  N={n}, T={t}, p={p}")
        print("   ", show("enumerated P(lifeless)", exact))
        print("   ", show("closed form (1-p)^N", closed))
        print("   ", show("Bernoulli lower bound 1 - N p", lower))
        print("   ", show("Bonferroni upper 1 - Np + (Np)^2/2", upper))
        assert exact == closed
        assert lower <= exact <= upper


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstration 4: the existence sandwich
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def demo_existence_sandwich() -> None:
    rule("4. EXISTENCE SANDWICH:  N p - (N p)^2 / 2 <= P(somebody) <= N p")
    print("  When N p is small, the Drake number IS the probability that")
    print("  anyone exists -- not a headcount.")
    for n, t, p in [(4, 3, Fraction(1, 10)), (3, 2, Fraction(1, 5)),
                    (6, 4, Fraction(1, 50))]:
        exact = probability(n, t, p, somebody_exists)
        e = drake_expectation(n, p)
        lower = e - e * e / 2
        print(f"\n  N={n}, T={t}, p={p}   (Drake expectation N p = {e})")
        print("   ", show("lower bound N p - (N p)^2 / 2", lower))
        print("   ", show("enumerated P(somebody exists)", exact))
        print("   ", show("upper bound N p", e))
        rel = float((e - exact) / e) if e else 0.0
        print(f"     relative error of the first-moment answer: {rel:.4%}")
        assert lower <= exact <= e


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstration 5: contact is quadratically rare, and decays like 1 / T
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def demo_contact() -> None:
    rule("5. CONTACT IS QUADRATICALLY RARE:  P(contact) <= (N^2 - N) p^2 / T")
    for n, t, p in [(3, 2, Fraction(1, 5)), (4, 3, Fraction(1, 10)),
                    (2, 5, Fraction(1, 2))]:
        exact = probability(n, t, p, has_contact)
        bound = contact_bound(n, t, p)
        ratio = float(bound / exact) if exact else float("inf")
        print(f"\n  N={n}, T={t}, p={p}")
        print("   ", show("enumerated P(contact)", exact))
        print("   ", show("proved bound (N^2 - N) p^2 / T", bound))
        print(f"      slack factor bound/exact = {ratio:.4f}")
        assert exact <= bound
    print("\n  (For N = 2 the slack is exactly 2: the union bound counts ORDERED pairs.)")

    print("\n  More time makes contact RARER -- T is in the denominator:")
    n, p = 3, Fraction(1, 5)
    for t in (2, 3, 4, 5, 6):
        exact = probability(n, t, p, has_contact)
        print(f"    N={n}, p={p}, T={t}:  P(contact) = {str(exact):>12} "
              f"= {float(exact):.6f}   (bound {float(contact_bound(n,t,p)):.6f})")

# Demonstration 6: lifetime is a linear lever, abundance a quadratic one
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def demo_lifetime_window() -> None:
    rule("6. LIFETIME WINDOWS:  P(contact_L) <= (N^2 - N)(2L - 1) p^2 / T")
    n, t, p = 3, 7, Fraction(1, 5)
    print(f"  N={n}, T={t}, p={p}\n")
    print(f"  {'L':>3}  {'exact P(contact_L)':>22}  {'proved bound':>16}  ok")
    for lifetime in (1, 2, 3, 4):
        exact = probability(n, t, p, lambda f, L=lifetime: has_window_contact(f, L))
        bound = window_contact_bound(n, t, p, lifetime)
        ok = exact <= bound
        print(f"  {lifetime:>3}  {float(exact):>22.8f}  {float(bound):>16.8f}  {ok}")
        assert ok

    print("\n  Compare the two levers at fixed L=1, doubling each parameter:")
    base = probability(3, 8, Fraction(1, 8), has_contact)
    dbl_p = probability(3, 8, Fraction(1, 4), has_contact)
    dbl_L = probability(3, 8, Fraction(1, 8), lambda f: has_window_contact(f, 2))
    print(f"    baseline (p=1/8, L=1)        : {float(base):.8f}")
    print(f"    doubling abundance (p=1/4)   : {float(dbl_p):.8f}"
          f"   ratio {float(dbl_p/base):.3f}  (~ quadratic, ~4x)")
    print(f"    doubling lifetime  (L=2)     : {float(dbl_L):.8f}"
          f"   ratio {float(dbl_L/base):.3f}  (~ linear,   ~3x = 2L-1)")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstration 7: the dual pigeonhole principle
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def demo_dual_pigeonhole() -> None:
    rule("7. DUAL PIGEONHOLE:  E[#empty epochs] >= T - N p")
    print("  Pointwise, an outcome with c civilizations leaves >= T - c epochs empty.")
    for n, t, p in [(3, 2, Fraction(1, 5)), (4, 3, Fraction(1, 10)),
                    (3, 6, Fraction(1, 4))]:
        exact = expectation(n, t, p, lambda f, T=t: empty_epoch_count(f, T))
        bound = empty_epochs_bound(n, t, p)
        print(f"\n  N={n}, T={t}, p={p}")
        print("   ", show("enumerated E[#empty epochs]", exact))
        print("   ", show("proved bound T - N p", bound))
        assert bound <= exact

        # pointwise check of the deterministic dual pigeonhole
        for f in enumerate_cosmoi(n, t):
            assert empty_epoch_count(f, t) >= t - civ_count(f)
        print("      pointwise dual pigeonhole E(f) >= T - X(f) verified on all "
              f"{(t+1)**n} outcomes.")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstration 8: pigeonhole thresholds are sharp
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def demo_pigeonhole_threshold() -> None:
    rule("8. THE PIGEONHOLE THRESHOLD c = T IS SHARP")
    print("  Contact is FORCED iff the number of civilizations exceeds the number")
    print("  of epochs.  Below the threshold, a contact-free schedule always exists.")
    print()
    print(f"  {'T':>3} {'c':>3}  {'forced?':>8}  {'contact-free schedule exists?':>32}")
    for t in (3, 4, 5):
        for c in range(1, t + 3):
            forced = c > t
            # a contact-free schedule is an injection {1..c} -> {1..T}

            print(f"  {t:>3} {c:>3}  {str(forced):>8}  {str(exists_free):>32}")
            assert forced != exists_free or c == 0
    print("\n  In the Fermi regime T ~ 4.5e9 while c is at most a handful:")
    print("  the forcing hypothesis fails by about NINE orders of magnitude.")

State = Optional[int]


def local_weight(state: State, n_epochs: int, p: Fraction) -> Fraction:
    """w(None) = 1 - p ;  w(e) = p / T for each of the T epochs."""
    return (Fraction(1) - p) if state is None else p / Fraction(n_epochs)


def all_states(n_epochs: int) -> List[State]:
    return [None] + list(range(n_epochs))


def enumerate_cosmoi(n_sites: int, n_epochs: int) -> Iterator[Outcome]:
    """Enumerate all (T+1)^N outcomes f : sites -> {None} u epochs."""
    yield from product(all_states(n_epochs), repeat=n_sites)


def outcome_weight(f: Outcome, n_epochs: int, p: Fraction) -> Fraction:
    w = Fraction(1)
    for state in f:
        w *= local_weight(state, n_epochs, p)
    return w


def exact_probability(
    n_sites: int, n_epochs: int, p: Fraction, event: Callable[[Outcome], bool]
) -> Fraction:
    """Exact probability of an arbitrary decidable event, by full enumeration.

    Cost: Theta(N * (T+1)^N) rational multiplications.
    """
    total = Fraction(0)
    for f in enumerate_cosmoi(n_sites, n_epochs):
        if event(f):
            total += outcome_weight(f, n_epochs, p)
    return total


def cylinder_probability(
    n_epochs: int, p: Fraction, allowed: Sequence[Sequence[State]]
) -> Fraction:
    """Cylinder factorization: P(f(i) in B_i for all i) = prod_i sum_{x in B_i} w(x).

    Cost: Theta(sum_i |B_i|) -- exponentially faster than enumeration.
    """
    result = Fraction(1)
    for block in allowed:
        result *= sum((local_weight(x, n_epochs, p) for x in block), Fraction(0))
    return result


def verify_factorization(n_sites: int, n_epochs: int, p: Fraction,
                         allowed: Sequence[Sequence[State]]) -> Dict[str, Fraction]:
    """Check the factorization theorem against brute-force enumeration."""
    blocks = [set(b) for b in allowed]

    def event(f: Outcome) -> bool:
        return all(f[i] in blocks[i] for i in range(n_sites))

    brute = exact_probability(n_sites, n_epochs, p, event)
    fast = cylinder_probability(n_epochs, p, allowed)
    return {"enumerated": brute, "factorized": fast, "difference": brute - fast}

    N, T, p = 3, 3, Fraction(1, 4)

    for key, val in report.items():
        print(f"{key:>12}: {val}  = {float(val):.10f}")
    assert report["difference"] == 0
    print("cylinder factorization verified exactly")

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from dataclasses import dataclass
from fractions import Fraction


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class FermiReport:
    """All first-moment quantities for a cosmos with N sites, T epochs, rate p."""

    n_sites: int
    n_epochs: int
    p: Fraction
    drake_expectation: Fraction
    lifeless_exact: float
    lifeless_lower: Fraction
    lifeless_upper: Fraction
    somebody_lower: Fraction
    somebody_upper: Fraction
    empty_epochs_lower: Fraction
    verdict: str

    def render(self) -> str:
        lines = [
            f"N = {self.n_sites}, T = {self.n_epochs}, p = {self.p}",
            f"  Drake expectation  E[X] = N p          = {float(self.drake_expectation):.6g}",
            f"  P(lifeless) = (1-p)^N                  = {self.lifeless_exact:.6g}",
            f"    Bernoulli lower bound 1 - N p        = {float(self.lifeless_lower):.6g}",
            f"    Bonferroni upper 1 - Np + (Np)^2/2   = {float(self.lifeless_upper):.6g}",
            f"  P(somebody exists) in "
            f"[{float(self.somebody_lower):.6g}, {float(self.somebody_upper):.6g}]",
            f"  E[#empty epochs] >= T - N p            = {float(self.empty_epochs_lower):.6g}"
            f"   (of {self.n_epochs})",
            f"  Verdict: {self.verdict}",
        ]
        return "\n".join(lines)


def drake_expectation(n_sites: int, p: Fraction) -> Fraction:
    """E[#civilizations] = N p exactly -- independent of the number of epochs."""
    return Fraction(n_sites) * p


def lifeless_probability(n_sites: int, p: Fraction) -> float:
    """P(no civilization anywhere) = (1 - p)^N.

    Evaluated as exp(N * log(1 - p)) so that astronomically large N (e.g. 10^10)
    costs O(1) rather than producing an exact rational with billions of digits.
    """
    if p == 1:
        return 0.0 if n_sites > 0 else 1.0
    return math.exp(n_sites * math.log1p(-float(p)))


def bernoulli_lower_bound(n_sites: int, p: Fraction) -> Fraction:
    """(1 - p)^N >= 1 - N p."""
    return Fraction(1) - Fraction(n_sites) * p


def bonferroni_upper_bound(n_sites: int, p: Fraction) -> Fraction:
    """(1 - p)^N <= 1 - N p + (N p)^2 / 2."""
    e = drake_expectation(n_sites, p)
    return Fraction(1) - e + e * e / 2


def analyse(n_sites: int, n_epochs: int, p: Fraction) -> FermiReport:
    """Assemble the full first-moment report and classify the regime.

    Cost: O(log N) rational operations -- no enumeration required, so the
    astronomically large parameters N = 1e10, T = 4.5e9 are handled instantly.
    """
    if not (0 <= p <= 1):
        raise ValueError("p must lie in [0, 1]")
    if n_epochs < 1:
        raise ValueError("there must be at least one epoch")

    e = drake_expectation(n_sites, p)
    lifeless = lifeless_probability(n_sites, p)
    lower = bernoulli_lower_bound(n_sites, p)
    upper = bonferroni_upper_bound(n_sites, p)

    if e < 1:
        verdict = (
            f"first-moment regime: emptiness is typical, "
            f"P(lifeless) >= {float(1 - e):.4g} > 0"
        )
    else:
        verdict = "crowded regime: the first moment exceeds one; bounds are vacuous"

    return FermiReport(
        n_sites=n_sites,
        n_epochs=n_epochs,
        p=p,
        drake_expectation=e,
        lifeless_exact=lifeless,
        lifeless_lower=lower,
        lifeless_upper=upper,
        somebody_lower=max(Fraction(0), e - e * e / 2),
        somebody_upper=min(Fraction(1), e),
        empty_epochs_lower=Fraction(n_epochs) - e,
        verdict=verdict,
    )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(analyse(10 ** 10, 4_500_000_000, Fraction(1, 10 ** 11)).render())
    print()
    print(analyse(4, 3, Fraction(1, 10)).render())

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from typing import Dict, List, Tuple


def window_fibre_size(n_epochs: int, epoch: int, lifetime: int) -> int:
    """Number of epochs b with |epoch - b| < lifetime, inside {0,...,T-1}."""
    lo = max(0, epoch - lifetime + 1)
    hi = min(n_epochs - 1, epoch + lifetime - 1)
    return hi - lo + 1


def count_window_pairs(n_epochs: int, lifetime: int) -> int:
    """Exact number of ordered epoch pairs (a, b) with |a - b| < L.

    Cost: O(T).  Always at most T * (2L - 1), the bound used in the theory.
    """
    return sum(window_fibre_size(n_epochs, e, lifetime) for e in range(n_epochs))


def pair_contact_bound(n_epochs: int, p: Fraction, lifetime: int) -> Fraction:
    """P(two prescribed distinct sites are mutually detectable) <= (2L-1) p^2 / T."""
    return Fraction(2 * lifetime - 1) * p * p / Fraction(n_epochs)


def contact_bound(n_sites: int, n_epochs: int, p: Fraction,
                  lifetime: int = 1) -> Fraction:
    """P(contact) <= (N^2 - N) (2L - 1) p^2 / T.

    Derivation: the exact two-site law gives P(f(i)=e, f(j)=e') = (p/T)^2; at most
    T(2L-1) epoch pairs are window-compatible, giving (2L-1)p^2/T per site pair; a
    union bound over the N^2 - N ordered site pairs finishes.
    Cost: O(1) rational operations.
    """
    if lifetime < 1:
        raise ValueError("lifetime must be at least one epoch")
    ordered_pairs = Fraction(n_sites) ** 2 - Fraction(n_sites)
    return ordered_pairs * pair_contact_bound(n_epochs, p, lifetime)


def contact_bound_via_expectation(n_sites: int, n_epochs: int, p: Fraction,
                                  lifetime: int = 1) -> Fraction:
    """Coarser form: P(contact) <= (N p)^2 (2L - 1) / T = E[X]^2 (2L-1) / T."""
    e = Fraction(n_sites) * p
    return e * e * Fraction(2 * lifetime - 1) / Fraction(n_epochs)


def lever_comparison(n_sites: int, n_epochs: int, p: Fraction,
                     lifetime: int) -> Dict[str, float]:
    """Quantify the asymmetry: abundance is quadratic, lifetime is linear."""
    base = contact_bound(n_sites, n_epochs, p, lifetime)
    double_p = contact_bound(n_sites, n_epochs, min(Fraction(1), 2 * p), lifetime)
    double_l = contact_bound(n_sites, n_epochs, p, 2 * lifetime)
    return {
        "baseline": float(base),
        "double_abundance_ratio": float(double_p / base) if base else float("nan"),
        "double_lifetime_ratio": float(double_l / base) if base else float("nan"),
    }


def contact_scan(n_sites: int, p: Fraction, lifetime: int,
                 epoch_counts: List[int]) -> List[Tuple[int, float]]:
    """Show the 1/T decay: more time means LESS contact."""
    return [(t, float(contact_bound(n_sites, t, p, lifetime))) for t in epoch_counts]

def outcome_weight(f: Outcome, n_epochs: int, p: Fraction) -> Fraction:
    w = Fraction(1)
    for s in f:
        w *= (Fraction(1) - p) if s is None else p / Fraction(n_epochs)
    return w


def has_contact(f: Outcome) -> bool:
    seen = set()
    for s in f:
        if s is None:
            continue
        if s in seen:
            return True
        seen.add(s)
    return False

        if has_contact(f):
            total += outcome_weight(f, n_epochs, p)
    return total

    return Fraction(n_sites ** 2 - n_sites) * p * p / Fraction(n_epochs)

    return k - 1;
  }
  // normal approximation for large means

  return Math.max(0, Math.round(lam + Math.sqrt(lam) * (u - 6)));

<p class="sub">No sampling, no approximation: this widget walks through <b>every one</b> of the
<code>(T+1)<sup>N</sup></code> possible universes, adds up their exact weights, and compares the
answers with the closed-form bounds. Watch the total mass stay pinned at exactly 1, watch the
expected civilization count land exactly on <code>N·p</code> no matter how many epochs you add, and
watch every proved inequality hold — usually with the factor-of-2 slack that comes from counting
ordered pairs of sites.</p>

<div class="wrap">

    <input type="range" id="sN" min="1" max="6" step="1" value="3">

    <input type="range" id="sT" min="1" max="6" step="1" value="3">
    <label>probability p <span class="val" id="lP">0.20</span></label>
    <input type="range" id="sP" min="0.01" max="0.9" step="0.01" value="0.20">
    <label>lifetime L <span class="val" id="lL">1</span></label>
    <input type="range" id="sL" min="1" max="6" step="1" value="1">
    <p class="note">Outcomes enumerated: <b id="cnt"></b><br>
    Each outcome assigns every site either <i>barren</i> (weight <code>1−p</code>) or a birth epoch
    (weight <code>p/T</code> each).</p>
  </div>

function enumerate(N, T, p, L){
  const states = T + 1;                 // index 0 = barren, 1..T = birth epoch
  const total = Math.pow(states, N);

    for (let i = 0; i < N; i++){

        if (Math.abs(f[i] - f[j]) < L) whit = true;
      }
    }
    if (hit) contact += w;
    if (whit) windowContact += w;
  }
  return {mass, expCiv, lifeless, somebody, contact, windowContact, expEmpty, total};
}

> *"Where is everybody?"* — Enrico Fermi, over lunch at Los Alamos, 1950.

The galaxy is old, huge, and — as far as we can tell — completely quiet. For seventy
years that quiet has been called a **paradox**, and an entire literature of exotic
explanations has grown up around it: Great Filters, zoo hypotheses, dark forests,
civilizations that reliably destroy themselves.

This page argues something less dramatic and much more precise. The silence is not an
anomaly. It is what the arithmetic predicts, and you can watch it predict it.

By the end you will be able to state and justify four things:

1. The Drake equation is an **average**, not a headcount.
2. When that average is below one, an empty universe is the **typical** outcome — and
   we can say by how much.
3. **Contact** is a second-order event: quadratic in abundance, *inversely* proportional
   to available time.
4. The pigeonhole principle, run in the right direction, predicts **empty holes**.

---

## 1. Two pigeons, and which way the principle points

The [pigeonhole principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pigeonhole_principle) is the
humblest theorem in mathematics: put more pigeons than holes into a loft and some hole
gets two pigeons. People reach for it in cosmic arguments all the time — *with so many
planets and so much time, surely somebody overlapped with us.*

That invocation has the orientation backwards. Pigeonhole forces a collision only when
the pigeons outnumber the holes. In the Fermi problem the pigeons are civilizations
(possibly fewer than one, in expectation) and the holes are the roughly
$4.5 \times 10^9$ years of cosmic history. The version that applies is the shadow of
the famous one:

> **Dual pigeonhole.** Place $c$ objects into $T$ boxes. At least $T - c$ boxes are empty.

Very few pigeons, unimaginably many holes. Most holes are empty. Hold that picture.

<details>
<summary><b>Why the dual form is trivially true (click to expand)</b></summary>

The occupied boxes are exactly the image of the placement map, and the image of a set
of size $c$ has at most $c$ elements. Complement within the $T$ boxes: at least
$T - c$ are untouched. No independence, no randomness, no assumptions. $\blacksquare$

</details>

---

## 2. Building a universe you can compute with

To say anything precise we need a model, and it should be the simplest one that is
honest. Here it is.

Fix three numbers: $N$ habitable **sites**, $T$ **epochs** of history (say one year
each), and $p$, the probability that a given site *ever* produces a technological
civilization.

An **outcome** is a function $f$ that assigns to each site either the symbol $\ast$
("never produced anyone") or a single epoch $e$ (the birth of its civilization). Sites
are independent. The weight of a single site's state is

$$
w(\ast) = 1 - p, \qquad w(e) = \frac{p}{T},
$$

and the weight of a whole universe is the product over its sites. Since
$(1-p) + T\cdot\frac{p}{T} = 1$, this is a genuine probability distribution on the
$(T+1)^N$ possible universes.

Everything below flows from a single identity.

> **Cylinder factorization.** If for each site $i$ you specify a set $B_i$ of allowed
> states, then
> $$\mathbb{P}\bigl(f(i) \in B_i \text{ for all } i\bigr) = \prod_{i=1}^{N}\ \sum_{x \in B_i} w(x).$$

Global questions become products of local answers.

<details>
<summary><b>Proof sketch of the factorization identity</b></summary>

The event is exactly the product set $B_1 \times \cdots \times B_N$. Its total weight
is $\sum_{f} \prod_i w(f(i))$ over that product set, and the distributive law for finite
products of finite sums — expanding $\prod_i \sum_{x \in B_i}$ into a sum over choice
functions — is precisely that sum. Outcomes outside the product set contribute nothing.
$\blacksquare$

</details>
